{"id": "20:11/q05", "question": "What kind of tree held the apparent fire?", "turns_on": "The reports identify the tree by different species; al-Būrsawī says the listed trees do not contain fire like other trees.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q05/p1", "position": "A jujube tree.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports a jujube in al-Wāḥidī and al-Ālūsī; al-Ṭabrisī reports him likewise. Al-Nasafī offers jujube or osage; al-Būrsawī lists jujube among several identifications."}, {"id": "20:11/q05/p2", "position": "An ʿawsaj or osage tree.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī allows osage; al-Būrsawī lists ʿawsaja; al-Ālūsī reports awsj."}, {"id": "20:11/q05/p3", "position": "A samura tree.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī lists green samura; al-Ālūsī transmits it from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd."}, {"id": "20:11/q05/p4", "position": "An al-ʿalīq or blackberry-like thorn tree.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī's list describes a blackberry-like thorn tree; al-Ālūsī's Wahb report calls the great green tree al-ʿalīq. These descriptions vary."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q06", "question": "What did the fire and tree look like together?", "turns_on": "Whether the fire preserved the green tree or consumed it.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q06/p1", "position": "Brilliant white fire or light appeared in a green tree without consuming it or being dimmed by its moisture.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, and al-Būrsawī describes the bright flame and living green tree; al-Rāzī says the glow ran bottom to top. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī describe white flame in green growth. Wahb in al-Ālūsī says the great flame grew without burning the tree."}, {"id": "20:11/q06/p2", "position": "The fire consumed the tree.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this interpretation from IK, R, Ṭ, Bg, and R, with reference to 20:10."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q07", "question": "How did the apparent fire behave as Moses approached?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q07/p1", "position": "It withdrew as he approached and came toward him when he drew back or stopped seeking it.", "reasons": "Wahb in al-Ṭabarī says Moses feared this motion. Al-Rāzī's Wahb report adds that Moses carried dry sticks, the fire repeatedly lured him, then vanished as a branch and dazzling light shone skyward. Al-Nasafī reports the reciprocal movement. Al-Ālūsī's Wahb report has repeated advance and retreat, a pillar of light reaching the sky, Moses' fear, angelic praise, and calm; it states no grading."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q08", "question": "What else did Moses perceive at the fire?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q08/p1", "position": "He saw intense light, heard angelic praise, and was awed before being calmed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Rāzī reports great light and angels glorifying God. Al-Būrsawī adds light too intense for the eyes, Moses covering his eyes, fear and astonishment, and subsequent calm. Wahb in al-Ālūsī also culminates his report in angelic praise and calm."}, {"id": "20:11/q08/p2", "position": "He found no person beside the fire.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī and Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by al-Būrsawī say no one was there."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q09", "question": "Was the phenomenon real fire or light?", "turns_on": "Whether the visible phenomenon was actual veiling fire or divine light perceived and named as fire.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q09/p1", "position": "It was light, called fire because Moses perceived it so.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī describes the fire as light. Al-Ālūsī reports Ibn ʿAbbās calling it light from God's light and Abū Ḥayyān preferring light to actual fire; he says al-Māwardī also adopts that view."}, {"id": "20:11/q09/p2", "position": "It was fire itself and one of God's veils.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. He also cites Abū Mūsā's Prophetic report that God's veil is fire and its unveiling would burn creatures reached by His face's radiance; al-Baghawī cites it and al-Khāzin says Muslim recorded it."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q10", "question": "How is Moses' fire classified by eating and drinking?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q10/p1", "position": "It neither eats nor drinks.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī and al-Ālūsī report a fourfold scheme: ordinary fire eats but does not drink, green-tree fire drinks but does not eat, Hellfire does both, and Moses' fire does neither."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q11", "question": "How is Moses' fire classified by light and burning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q11/p1", "position": "It gives light without burning.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī and al-Ālūsī report a fourfold contrast: ordinary fire has both light and burning, Hellfire burns without light, and Moses' fire shines without burning. Al-Būrsawī says trees have neither; al-Ālūsī specifies tree fire as neither."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q12", "question": "What happened with Moses' sandals when he arrived?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q12/p1", "position": "He removed sandals made from the hide of an unritually dead donkey.", "reasons": "Muqātil says God ordered their removal at Tuwa; Qatāda as reported by Yaḥyā says Moses removed them and then approached."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q13", "question": "What does nūdiya mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q13/p1", "position": "He was told or addressed.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās uses 'he was told' to explain the variant readings of yā Mūsā annī. Al-Nasafī and Asad give the literal passive sense 'he was called.'"}]}
{"id": "20:11/q14", "question": "What is the passive subject of nūdiya?", "turns_on": "Whether the passive promotes Moses, an understood verbal noun, or the quoted clause; the last is challenged because a clause cannot be the subject.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q14/p1", "position": "Its implicit subject is Moses.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī in al-Ṭabrisī allows Moses because he was already mentioned. Al-Samīn prefers this, as does al-Ālūsī as the apparent reading."}, {"id": "20:11/q14/p2", "position": "An implicit verbal noun is the subject: the calling occurred.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this proposal; al-Samīn calls the equivalent 'the call was called' weak. Abū ʿAlī in al-Ṭabrisī also allows an implicit pronoun rather than the quoted clause."}, {"id": "20:11/q14/p3", "position": "The quoted words yā Mūsā function as the subject.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports that the call is taken to include speech and the quoted wording to be its intended message. Abū ʿAlī in al-Ṭabrisī and al-Samīn object that a clause cannot be a passive subject."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q15", "question": "How is the quoted address attached to nūdiya?", "turns_on": "Whether 'called' itself introduces speech or an omitted verb of saying is supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q15/p1", "position": "Calling itself has the force of saying, so the words are the call's speech.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this construction to the Kūfans."}, {"id": "20:11/q15/p2", "position": "An unspoken verb 'he was told' introduces the quoted address.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes the omitted saying verb to the Basrans: Moses was called and told 'O Moses.' Al-Naḥḥās glosses nūdiya as 'he was told.'"}]}
{"id": "20:11/q16", "question": "What effect does the passive wording of nūdiya have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q16/p1", "position": "Concealing the caller makes the summons greater when Moses is named.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī points to the sequence from an unnamed caller to Moses' explicit name. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the passive withholds the unknown caller's identity to heighten anticipation; the following 'I am your Lord' reveals who spoke to Moses."}, {"id": "20:11/q16/p2", "position": "Omitting the agent subtly suggests the sign appeared suddenly to Moses.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links the passive's omission to the sudden appearance of the sign."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q17", "question": "Who produced the call to Moses?", "turns_on": "Whether God's address was unmediated or made audible through light.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q17/p1", "position": "God addressed Moses directly and alone.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this view."}, {"id": "20:11/q17/p2", "position": "God made His inseparable light voice the call.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports that the light spoke to calm Moses enough to bear God's command."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q18", "question": "From where was the call heard?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q18/p1", "position": "From the tree or its vicinity.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī says Moses heard the tree call; Wahb in al-Ṭabrisī says Moses heard a voice without seeing its place. Al-Qurṭubī specifies the tree's direction and vicinity and compares Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ. Study Quran reports God called from a tree in the valley."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q19", "question": "How did Moses know the caller was his Lord?", "turns_on": "Whether recognition at the first revelation requires evidentiary inference or is immediate in the experience of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q19/p1", "position": "He recognized God by a miracle or divinely created knowledge.", "reasons": "Wahb in al-Ṭabrisī says Moses heard but could not locate the voice and knew the caller by the response and a miracle. Abū Ḥayyān allows knowledge created by God or a miracle; he says Muʿtazilites require miraculous proof because necessary knowledge would conflict with accountability."}, {"id": "20:11/q19/p2", "position": "Revelation gave immediate certainty of the divine speaker.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the addressee apprehends no other speaker, citing the Quran's account of divine communication at 42:51. A prophet's first reception of mission must be immediate; acquired rational proof would not be reception from the unseen. He says an unseen veil or intermediary is compatible with this experience, citing 19:52, 28:30, and 20:13."}]}

rophetic commission as his own precursor miracle.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q20/p1", "position": "It is an irhāṣ, a precursor miracle.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī classifies the pre-prophetic marvel this way and says Muʿtazilites reject it."}, {"id": "20:11/q20/p2", "position": "A miracle cannot occur before Moses' commission unless it belongs to another prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this Muʿtazilite objection."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q21", "question": "How is annī or innī in the following divine speech read and construed?", "turns_on": "Whether the hamza has fatḥa and attaches the following clause to the call, or kasra and starts quoted speech; reports differ on the named readers and nuances of attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q21/p1", "position": "With fatḥa, annī: he was called with or because of the words 'I am your Lord.'", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Naḥḥās take an to be accusative; Abū ʿAlī in al-Ṭabrisī says calling can take a preposition. Al-Jishumī glosses 'because I am your Lord.' Named readers vary: al-Naḥḥās includes al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, Abū ʿAmr; al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī list Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr; al-Kashshāf lists Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr. Abū Ḥayyān gives Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr's wa-annī."}, {"id": "20:11/q21/p2", "position": "With kasra, innī begins direct quoted speech: 'O Moses, I am your Lord.'", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Jishumī, al-Kashshāf, Abū ʿAlī in al-Ṭabrisī, and Abū Ḥayyān describe a fresh quotation or supplied saying verb; Abū Ḥayyān calls it the majority reading. Al-Farrāʾ allows the call to include annī and Mūsā. Al-Naḥḥās reports an interpretation in which Moses says 'I am.'"}]}
{"id": "20:11/q22", "question": "Is the final yāʾ of innī opened or left still?", "turns_on": "The reported recitation of the final yāʾ in the following innī.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q22/p1", "position": "Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Abū ʿAmr open the final yāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives this reader list."}, {"id": "20:11/q22/p2", "position": "The remaining readers leave the final yāʾ quiescent.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī contrasts them with the four who open it."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q23", "question": "How does this call connect with other accounts of Moses' call?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q23/p1", "position": "It is the call from the blessed spot at the valley's right side and from the tree.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr compares 28:30. Al-Qurṭubī also refers to Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ for the direction of the call. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 19:52, 28:30, and 20:13 to say an intermediary or veil can accompany divine revelation."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q24", "question": "What inward significance is given to Moses' encounter and call?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q24/p1", "position": "The divine call enveloped Moses and overwhelmed his selfhood; God alone bears and answers His own address.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar in al-Sulamī says every hair perceived the call from every direction, awe and majesty confirmed it, and God's self-identification left Moses stunned and annihilated as an intermediary locus."}, {"id": "20:11/q24/p2", "position": "The fire is a veil of majesty through which God's manifestation addresses Moses.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says Moses connects with the fire and is called beyond fiery curtains; 'I am your Lord' is the divine manifestation in fiery form."}, {"id": "20:11/q24/p3", "position": "Fire figures ardent love and its light dissolves Moses' selfhood into single-hearted orientation.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī distinguishes light as love from fire as longing: their fullness lets essential light appear as attribute-fire and burn away selfhood."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q25", "question": "What do qabas and miqbās mean in the preceding request for fire?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q25/p1", "position": "Qabas is a flame; miqbās is a firebrand or tool for taking fire.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī supplies these lexical meanings in the discussion attached to the call."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q26", "question": "Can verbs from qabas describe taking both fire and knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether the two verbal forms keep fire and knowledge distinct or both extend to either.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q26/p1", "position": "The uses are distinguished: qabastu is for fire, while aqbastu someone knowledge is for seeking knowledge for that person.", "reasons": "Al-Yazīdī as reported by al-Qurṭubī draws this distinction. Al-Qurṭubī also says qabistu and iqtibās can mean taking fire, while iqtibās can mean acquiring knowledge."}, {"id": "20:11/q26/p2", "position": "Both aqbastuhu and qabastuhu can apply to fire or knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī as reported by al-Qurṭubī permits both verbs for either object. Al-Qurṭubī also notes iqtibās can refer to fire-taking or knowledge acquisition."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q27", "question": "What does hudā mean in the preceding search?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q27/p1", "position": "It means hādiyan, a guide.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī supplies the gloss."}]}
{"id": "20:11/q28", "question": "What view of divine istiwāʾ is noted in the preceding discussion?", "turns_on": "Whether istiwāʾ is understood as power or as a distinct act or attribute; al-Jishumī says the latter is unintelligible.", "positions": [{"id": "20:11/q28/p1", "position": "It means power.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī prefers Abū ʿAlī's view as sounder and finds the Kullābī account unintelligible."}, {"id": "20:11/q28/p2", "position": "It is an act or attribute called istiwāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī attributes this to the Kullābīs and calls it unintelligible."}]}
{"id": "20:12/q01", "question": "How is إني read and construed after the call?", "turns_on": "Whether the particle begins direct speech or is syntactically governed by the call; the final yāʾ also varies.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q01/p1", "position": "Kasra: direct quoted speech after Moses was called.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari prefers it because يا موسى intervenes; al-Farisi cites the ensuing direct quotations at 20:13–14. Basrans posit an omitted قول; Kufans treat نادى as speech. Abu Ubayd chooses the common reading. Nafi opens the final yāʾ while other kasra readers generally quiet it; the two Medinese readers, Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr open it in the five annexed yāʾs enumerated by Ibn al-Jazari. Ibn Mujahid gives the surrounding first-person-yāʾ patterns: Nāfiʿ opens those listed except ولي فيها and أخي اشدد; Abū ʿAmr quiets ولي فيها and حشرتني أعمى; Ibn Kathīr quiets ولي فيها, ويسر لي أمري, لذكري إن, على عيني إذ and برأسي إني; Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim through Abū Bakr quiet all those listed."}, {"id": "20:12/q01/p2", "position": "Fatḥa: a subordinate statement giving the content or cause of the call.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr, also Abu Jafar in several lists, read annī; the yāʾ is open. Al-Zajjaj gives the clause accusative position; others supply bi with نودي, supported by a poetic ناديت باسم example. Ibn Atiyya allows causal 'because'; al-Samin finds it weak, and al-Alusi finds the intervening vocative awkward. Al-Alusi instead supplies أعلم. Qiraat-ER offers 'Know that I am your Lord'. Ibn al-Jazari finds no explicit report for inferring Abu Jafar's yāʾ vowel. Al-Farisi adds that neither quoted clause can serve as deputy subject of passive نودي; the earlier Moses can. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the omitted preposition yields 'he was called that I am your Lord' and that the emphasis remains in either reading."}]}
{"id": "20:12/q02", "question": "What grammatical role does أنا play?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q02/p1", "position": "It can be a subject, an emphasis, or a separator.", "reasons": "Al-Samin says it may be a subject with ربك as predicate, an emphasis of the first-person pronoun, or a separator."}]}
{"id": "20:12/q03", "question": "Why repeat the first-person pronoun in إني أنا ربك?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q03/p1", "position": "The repetition confirms the speaker's identity and removes Moses' doubt.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari calls it strengthened proof and secure recognition; Ibn al-Jawzi compares 15:89. Al-Tabarsi, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Alusi and Bursevi likewise stress certainty."}]}
{"id": "20:12/q04", "question": "Why say 'your Lord' here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q04/p1", "position": "It marks a direct, personal audience with Moses and fits this sura's focus on his worship and mission.", "reasons": "Tabatabai contrasts the later 'I am Allah,' which states the revealed message. Al-Samarrai contrasts al-Naml and al-Qasas, which say 'Lord of the worlds'; Ta Ha directly instructs Moses in worship and prayer, promises signs and recounts his life."}, {"id": "20:12/q04/p2", "position": "'Your Lord' reassures Moses before an unseen speaker, since a lord cares gently for the one under his care.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says this personal address calmed Moses' fear of the unseen voice."}]}
{"id": "20:12/q05", "question": "How did Moses know who was speaking?", "turns_on": "Whether revelation itself supplies certainty or Moses needs an inferential sign.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q05/p1", "position": "God gave Moses immediate, necessary certainty in revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi favors knowledge created in Moses without inference. Tabatabai says a prophet's initial revelation is directly certain; 42:51 frames divine communication, and rational proof would make prophecy an acquired inference."}, {"id": "20:12/q05/p2", "position": "He inferred divine identity from a miracle or distinctive signs.", "reasons": "The Mu'tazila require a miracle because necessary knowledge would remove moral responsibility; al-Alusi records prior or later miracle views and questions whether unique-sounding attributes alone withstand satanic suggestion. A report from Wahb says the omnidirectional voice and God's nearness assured Moses; other reports describe hearing from all six directions and through

{"id": "20:12/q06", "question": "How was God's speech heard by Moses?", "turns_on": "The nature of divine speech and whether an audible form is direct, created, or a representation of inner speech.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q06/p1", "position": "Moses heard God's own eternal verbal speech directly, without an intermediary.", "reasons": "A Sunni group in al-Alusi says successive letters need temporal sequence only with an organ such as a tongue; without one the speech can be heard at once."}, {"id": "20:12/q06/p2", "position": "He heard created sound in the tree, while God's speech remains eternal.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi attributes this to Sunni scholars of Transoxiana."}, {"id": "20:12/q06/p3", "position": "The divine verbal speech was originated.", "reasons": "Groups al-Alusi calls innovators differ over whether events can subsist in God; those denying this locate the created sound in a body."}, {"id": "20:12/q06/p4", "position": "He spiritually received inner speech that was later represented as words.", "reasons": "Al-Ashari describes hearing beyond letters, sound and rational comprehension; another account compares familiar word forms produced in intellect and common sense to a dream. {"id": "20:12/q07", "question": "Can this command coexist with eternal divine speech?", "turns_on": "Whether an eternal command can have an addressee who comes to exist later.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q07/p1", "position": "An eternal imperative to Moses before his existence is absurd.", "reasons": "The Mu'tazila compare it to addressing absent people in an empty house."}, {"id": "20:12/q07/p2", "position": "God's speech is eternal but was not an imperative or prohibition in eternity.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports this first reply from his school."}, {"id": "20:12/q07/p3", "position": "The eternal speech is already an order, and Moses later becomes its addressee without a change in it.", "reasons": "Al-Razi's school compares eternal divine power yielding capacity for action later."}]}
{"id": "20:12/q08", "question": "How does ف connect the sandal command to the declaration?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q08/p1", "position": "The command follows as a consequence of the declaration of God's lordship.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the preceding self-identification motivates removing the sandals. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the sequence signals that the divine speech itself made the place sacred."}]}
{"id": "20:12/q09", "question": "What do اخلع and نعل mean literally?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q09/p1", "position": "The command is to take off the two coverings of Moses' feet.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi gives khalaʿ as remove and naʿl as a foot covering; Abu Hayyan says it can be leather, iron, or wood. {"id": "20:12/q10", "question": "What were Moses' sandals made of?", "turns_on": "Whether the footwear was impure donkey hide, pure cowhide, or divinely created.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q10/p1", "position": "They were made of hide from an unritually dead donkey, often said to be untanned.", "reasons": "Qatada, Ka'b, Ali, Ikrima and others transmit it; Ibn Masud attributes a report to the Prophet. Al-Tabari says that report's chain needs scrutiny; al-Tirmidhi calls it gharīb and al-Qurtubi distinguishes the weak Kufan Humayd ibn Ali from trustworthy Meccan Humayd ibn Qays. Al-Alusi calls the transmitted report unusual. Some say donkey hide without specifying carrion. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifically cites al-Tirmidhī's transmission from Ibn Masʿūd attributing the dead-donkey-hide report to the Prophet."}, {"id": "20:12/q10/p2", "position": "They were ritually pure or slaughtered cowhide.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others give this alternative; Kashifi explicitly prefers processed cowhide."}, {"id": "20:12/q10/p3", "position": "God created the sandals.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan records this report along with Moses casting them beyond the valley."}]}
{"id": "20:12/q11", "question": "Why was Moses told to remove the sandals?", "turns_on": "Whether the command responds to impure footwear, direct contact with blessing, reverent decorum, or the end of a practical need.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q11/p1", "position": "Their dead-animal hide was impure and should not enter the sacred valley.", "reasons": "Al-Muqatil, Ka'b, Qatada and others identify carrion donkey hide. {"id": "20:12/q15", "question": "Does the sandal command govern prayer or mosque footwear?", "turns_on": "Whether Moses' occasion-specific command supplies a general rule for worship footwear.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q15/p1", "position": "It gives no general objection to praying or circumambulating in clean sandals.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says the valley's honor made the order specific; the Prophet prayed in sandals, removed them only after Gabriel reported soil, and questioned those who imitated him. {"id": "20:12/q18", "question": "What does المقدس mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjective emphasizes purification or blessing; some sources combine them.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q18/p1", "position": "Purified and set apart from impurity or evil.", "reasons": "Qutrub and Ibn Atiyya give 'purified'; al-Qurtubi derives it from quds, purity, and relates holy land to God removing unbelievers and settling believers. {"id": "20:12/q19", "question": "Why is this valley sacred?", "turns_on": "Whether the ground's holiness follows a specific divine association or the land's purification alone.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q19/p1", "position": "God specially favored it through His call, revelation or prescribed worship there.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi says God can favor places, times and creatures; merely removing unbelievers cannot explain this valley's distinct holiness. {"id": "20:12/q21", "question": "What does Ṭuwā mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether Ṭuwā is a place name, a doubled sanctification or call, an act of treading or crossing, a night expression, or a personal name.", "positions": [{"id": "20:12/q21/p1", "position": "It is the proper name of the valley.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others identify it as a name; Ibn Zayd calls it ancient. {"id": "20:13/q02", "question": "How does the clause 'and I chose you' connect grammatically to the preceding speech?", "turns_on": "The vowel of the initial hamza and whether the clause coordinates with the preceding call, resumes speech, or supplies an implied cause.", "positions": [{"id": "20:13/q02/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with the preceding declaration of God's lordship or call to Moses.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ attaches the singular clause to nūdiya; Ibn Khālawayh continues the open-hamza plural from 'I am your Lord' in 20:12. {"id": "20:13/q04", "question": "For what did God choose Moses?", "turns_on": "Whether the choice confers the prophetic mission here or marks an earlier stage in an inward sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "20:13/q04/p1", "position": "For prophethood and messengership, including the privilege of divine speech.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā, al-Kalbī, al-Baghawī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr and the Study Quran explicitly include the message, speech, or both; the Study Quran connects direct address with Moses' title Kalīm Allāh. {"id": "20:13/q05", "question": "From among whom was Moses chosen?", "turns_on": "The unstated comparison group: all humanity, Moses' people, or those alive in his time.", "positions": [{"id": "20:13/q05/p1", "position": "From humanity at large.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives humanity as one scope of God's selection."}, {"id": "20:13/q05/p2", "position": "From his own people.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says a second object of ikhtartuka is omitted, yielding 'I chose you from among your people'; al-Ālūsī also gives this narrower scope."}, {"id": "20:13/q05/p3", "position": "Above all people alive in Moses' time.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr grounds the temporal scope and distinction in 7:144, where God selects Moses above the people by His messages and words."}]}
